paper_sections.title: Cognitive and neural contributors to emotion regulation in aging

description.value: The study examined how younger and older adults use cognitive reappraisal to regulate emotional responses, focusing on age-related differences in brain activation, amygdala-prefrontal connectivity, and the contribution of individual cognitive ability.

design.value: Twenty older adults and 22 younger adults completed psychometric testing and training in one session and an event-related cognitive reappraisal task during fMRI scanning in a second session on a different day. On each trial, participants viewed positive, negative, or neutral pictures and either experienced their emotions naturally or reappraised the picture to decrease their emotional response.

Participants recalled as many of the previously presented words as possible after a 20-min delay.
Participants evaluated whether each of 16 target words and 16 lure words was old or new.
Participants pressed the spacebar every time a white square appeared in the middle of the screen; performance was calculated as mean reaction time for correct choices.
Participants pressed the corresponding left or right button when shown arrows pointing left or right; performance was calculated as mean reaction time for correct choices.

Participants responded to the color of words presented in red or blue text; performance included accuracy on congruent trials minus accuracy on incongruent trials and the reaction-time difference between incongruent and congruent trials.

Participants listened to strings of numbers and recited each string back in backward order; the task continued until errors on two consecutive trials.

task_description.value: Each trial began with a single photographic image that was negative, positive, or neutral in valence. Participants viewed the image for 2 s, received a 2-s verbal cue to experience their emotions naturally or to decrease their emotional response by reappraising the image, and then continued implementing the cued strategy during a 6-s delay period. At the end of each trial, participants rated the image's valence.

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to experience the emotions evoked by the image naturally or to decrease their emotional response to the image by reappraising it, using a strategy of thinking of themselves as an emotionally detached and objective third party.

stimuli.value: Positive, neutral, or negative photographic images drawn from the International Affective Picture System. Positive images had mean valence 7.3, neutral images 5.1, and negative images 2.5; positive and negative images were matched for arousal.

task_performance_measures.value: self-reported affective valence using an 8-option non-verbal Manikin scale

description.value: Functional data were collected across six runs, each containing 238 imaging volumes. The first six volumes from each run were removed to allow stabilization of the T2 signal.

structured_details.value: {"field_of_view_mm": 240, "flip_angle_degrees": 90, "slices": 34, "slice_orientation": "axial slices parallel to the AC-PC plane", "runs": 6, "volumes_per_run": 238}

description.value: An initial high-resolution inversion-recovery-prepared SPGR anatomical scan was acquired to aid with co-registration and normalization, with whole-brain coverage and approximately 1 mm3 voxel size.

The fMRI data underwent motion correction, slice-timing correction, removal of non-brain voxels, spatial smoothing, high-pass temporal filtering, run exclusion based on excessive motion, registration to high-resolution anatomical images, and normalization to the MNI template.

steps.value: removal of non-brain voxels using BET
spatial smoothing with a Gaussian kernel of FWHM 6 mm
runs with more than five volumes with greater than 1 mm of movement in any direction were excluded
registration to high-resolution anatomical images using FLIRT
normalization to the Montreal Neurologic Institute template image using FLIRT

model_settings.value: The model examined effects of age group (younger, older), regulation condition (‘Reappraise’, ‘Experience’), and stimulus category (positive, negative) upon self-reported valence.

The first regression model created five regressors of interest for Experience-Positive, Experience-Negative, Experience-Neutral, Reappraise-Positive, and Reappraise-Negative. These modeled the 8-s period of experiencing or reappraising emotional content using a unit amplitude function. Additional nuisance regressors modeled the 2-s visual presentation and the response period. Analyses used whole-brain-corrected thresholds of voxel significance z > 2.3 and cluster significance corrected to P < 0.05. Age group was introduced as a covariate at the third-level across-subjects analysis for whole-brain comparisons.

software.value: FEAT Version 5.98, part of FSL (FMRIB's Software Library)

model_settings.value: The model included activation time courses from the left and right amygdala, a boxcar task regressor weighted positively for Reappraise trials and negatively for Experience trials, and two interaction regressors created from the convolution of amygdala activation and the task regressor. Amygdala time courses were extracted from functionally defined ROIs using the conjunction of Reappraise > Experience contrasts for positive and negative stimuli.

The relationship between activation changes in each ROI in the Reappraisal versus Experience contrast and the cognitive composite score was examined while controlling for the effects of age upon both cognition and ROI activation.

interpretations.value: A similar pattern of activation was found when examining trials involving negative images; reappraisal of negative images evoked increased activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, along with the inferior parietal lobule.
